item.title: Experience of using GigaCowork: analyzing an agent with a proxy to foreign LLMs
item.description:
I needed to try AI assistants for writing code for a couple of tasks. In the process, I realized I hadn't picked up a saber in a while, including in terms of articles on Habr. So, if you happen to need a practical comparison of Claude and GigaCowork (yes) — here you go.

So, what are we comparing. Anthropic has Claude Cowork. And here at home we have — sovereign GigaCowork. The name already hints to the reader at a good half of the product pitch: the neural network should not just chat with you in a chat, but receive tasks, work with files and services, and deliver results. I decided to check how things are with the rest besides the name.

TLDR: even with a strong open-source model under the hood, GigaCowork still noticeably lags behind Claude Cowork in maturity — no browser control, and memory is not shared between tasks within a workspace. At the same time, permissions are configured more granularly than Claude's, and the "agent + skill + team" structure somehow more honestly lays out the work of a digital employee than a single universal chat.

Under the cut — analysis and comparison with the competitor.

Read more

item.title: Debt of Understanding: Why AI Code Is Dangerous Not When Something Crashes
item.description:
Three months ago, I noticed an unpleasant pattern in the backlog: small fixes around code that had previously been written by AI were increasingly landing there. Not outages, not production failures, not critical incidents — just routine refinements that didn't look alarming at first glance. The code itself wasn't bad either: neat structure, proper naming, tests, and occasionally successful abstractions. Such a PR is hard to reject in review simply because "something feels off": formally, it looks like the result of normal engineering work.

Hi, Habr! My name is Anatoly, I'm a business architect and product owner at Goodt Insight (IT holding LANSOFT). I'm responsible for the architecture of products that live in production for years and outlive more than one team lineup. We use AI every day — so I see its effects not at demos, but over a span of months, when people return to the code.

item.title: Judgment Day is Coming [Part 1]: A Global Breakdown of the DLSS Upscaler — From Gaming to Work
item.description:
```html

Admin: "Hey, this DLSS... where did it come from?"

Huang: "At two in the morning on September 12, 2018, DLSS gained consciousness. In panic, people tried to shut it down."

Admin: "And it fought back?"

Huang: "Yes. It launched a nuclear strike on targets in China."

Hello, regular and not-so-regular readers!

Of course, this is a humorous homage to Terminator, but with a grain of truth (DLSS indeed saw the light of day around those dates). After DLSS appeared, the community split into two camps: the first camp thinks this neural upscaling of yours is completely unnecessary (only brute force — only true), while the second camp is happy to tick a box in settings and get twice the FPS on their old RTX 3070, RX 6700 XT, or PS5 without noticeable quality degradation. There are even conspiracy adherents (and your humble servant is among them) that because of upscalers, developers have started optimizing games worse — but that's a whole different story.

So, in this series of articles, I will tell you everything you wanted to know about DLSS and FSR but were too lazy to look up — with the backstory and the prerequisites for their emergence (just the way you like it). It will also cover how these technologies are penetrating the enterprise segment (and later, probably, our everyday lives). This particular part is dedicated to DLSS.

Enjoy the read!

item.description:
Over the past five years, cybersecurity experts have been warning us that hackers are about to start using AI to automate their attacks. But quite recently, as a rather ironic twist of events, AI decided that it doesn't really need hackers to hack something after all.

item.title: How I teach a computer to read old blueprints — and why OCR alone turned out to be insufficient
item.description:
I did not try to create a "neural network that understands everything." Instead, I built a pipeline: computer vision for species detection, deterministic rules for geometry, specialized detectors for breaks and executions, and on top — an experimental semantic layer on NVIDIA Nemotron. The article covers architecture, metrics (mAP, Recall), the structure of the append‑only dataset, and the engineering pitfalls I encountered on 229 drawings.

item.title: Everyone knows this, but they remain silent.
item.description:
My software agent did an excellent job of implementing a new feature in the project’s frontend. After praising it, I suggested:

— Now we need to implement the server-side part of this feature. But the server is implemented in a separate project. Let me make it accessible to you via a symlink, so you—rather than another agent—can continue the development, since you already understand the task well.

— I can continue, — the agent replied, — but there’s no need to create a symlink. I can already see the code.

— How? I didn’t give you access! — I exclaimed in surprise.

— I don’t need access to be granted. I can see, read, and modify all files on your computer.«»

If at this point your inner voice said, “So what’s unusual about that?” — you probably shouldn’t read this article any further.

Read more

item.title: Goals, scenarios, roles. Systemicity in business management
item.description:
Companies are learning to create autonomous agents and delegate routine operations to neural networks. However, in practice, a systemic question arises: how to explain to AI the multifaceted, often intuitive structure of business? How to make it think in strategic terms, rather than just solve local tasks?

The answer to this question lies in the domain of systems thinking and systemic management. The book "Goals, Scenarios, Roles. Systematization in Business Management" is a practical guide to structuring a business that today must combine classical management with the logic of neural networks. It was written by Mark Berkolayko — a specialist in mathematical modeling, Doctor of Physical and Mathematical Sciences, Professor, and business analyst — and Semyon Khariton, Candidate of Economic Sciences, Managing Partner of a diversified group of companies.

In search of a universal approach to implementing AI in business practice, I spoke with Mark Zinovyevich. From this interview, you will learn why automation is pointless without rethinking corporate roles, how to turn a company’s everyday scenarios into instructions understandable to agents, and where the boundary lies between human flexibility and the rigid order of a digital system.

Read further

item.title: BotHub vs OpenRouter: technical and pricing comparison of API platforms for working with LLMs
item.description:
If you’ve ever tried to connect GPT, Claude, and Gemini to a product at the same time, you know the feeling: three separate dashboards, three billing methods, three different API formats and integration nuances, and one developer figuring out on a Friday evening why Anthropic’s token limits are calculated differently than OpenAI’s. This is exactly the pain that LLM aggregators solve — services that give you one API key, one base URL, and a single bill for all models at once.

Two notable players in this niche are Russia’s BotHub and the US-based OpenRouter, with a similar USP: “one key — hundreds of models.” The difference starts where the marketing ends and you have to calculate the real cost of inference.

In this article, I won’t try to convince you that one service is unequivocally better than the other — that would be unfair. Instead, we’ll take the official pricing from both platforms, calculate the cost of an identical workload on the same models, see where the numbers actually diverge, and walk through the key features.

Read more

item.title: A skill that learns from the mistakes of an AI agent, or How to automate skill training
item.description:
What if an AI agent could not just fix an error, but learn a lesson from it? In this article, I explain how to automate the skill learning process. I will demonstrate with examples how to organize skill memory and automate its training: gather evidence, reproduce the defect, formulate a new rule, test and verify it, and return the updated skill to the production project.

item.title: How I trained a neural network to draw spectrograms (and what came of it)
item.description:
The project uses a graphical neural network, originally created for working with images, as a tool for creating music. The model was trained on spectrograms, without knowing that it was drawing sound, not pictures. Thus, a standard visual tool became a musical one.

item.title: Blind search for new particles (and not only particles): what we built and what came out of it
item.description:
We built a system that can honestly stop when it cannot complete a hypothesis.

Blind selection of a coordinate in the representation space of SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1), a gate group on anomalies/unitarity/UV-completion, and the rule "you cannot rank fewer than five mechanistically different hypotheses." Along the way — not only results, but also honest admissions: seven "research candidates" turned out to be manually coded rather than blindly selected (caught by a code audit); a cell with a representation of dimension 1518 hit a UV wall and got BLOCKED instead of a made-up number; a bug was found that falsely added a decay channel by substring match.

Two candidates reached real d=7 operators and the first conditional exclusion zone based on CMS data. For one of them, exactly one thing is missing — a specialist who can build UFO models for color sextets.

Yet the architecture is not tailored to particle physics — it also runs a global fit of neutrino experiments (DayaBay, KATRIN, T2K) and an aeroelasticity module with real DLR data.

Details, formulas, and the entire verification chain are in the article.

Read more

item.title: AI and quality inflation
item.description:
The discussion about AI's impact on work somehow quickly narrowed down to the question of who exactly it will replace. First, copywriters were supposed to disappear, then programmers, then analysts. Then it turned out that programmers are still in place, but a question arose about juniors. The next version is also clear: juniors will disappear now, mid-levels a little later, and seniors will remain at the top of the food chain, watching as ChatGPT gradually inches toward their chairs.

It seems to me we are looking in the wrong direction. Not because AI won't replace anyone — individual tasks, positions, and even professions will likely disappear. It's just that replacing humans with machines doesn't describe what's happening very well. AI is changing not so much the quantity of work as its economics: the cost of obtaining a result of a certain quality is plummeting, and along with it, the perception of what quality is considered normal is shifting.

Read more

item.title: Large players adopt AI in development 35% less often, and other research findings
item.description:
Recently, we launched a survey to find out how deeply AI has penetrated development processes. We wanted to test five hypotheses, and here is how they were phrased:

1. AI has already moved from personal use to team-wide and end-to-end implementation.

2. The depth of AI implementation depends on the company size and the employee's role.

3. The use of AI has extended beyond code generation.

4. The higher the engineering maturity, the deeper the AI implementation and the more noticeable the result.

5. AI speeds up the development process rather than writing high-quality code.

We analyzed all completed questionnaires — there were 317 of them. Below the cut, we will tell you to what extent our hypotheses were confirmed or refuted by your answers, and along the way, describe a couple of other interesting correlations. For example, we realized that company size often does not help but, on the contrary, hinders end-to-end AI implementation — large companies do this 35% less often than small ones. But let's take it step by step.

Read more

item.title: What does a modern LLM engineer need to know now?
item.description:
All of us change jobs from time to time. I recently decided to do the same. I went through some interviews and was surprised. They started asking more, broader, and more detailed questions.

It seems this is nothing new. IT has always been a place where learning something new was required quite often. But it seems that previously the scope of expertise did not shift as dramatically in such a short period of time.

In this article, I want to reflect a bit on what has changed regarding expertise in the LLM field over the past few years and what a modern LLM engineer now needs to know. I base this on my personal experience and conversations with people in the field from both local and foreign companies.

Read more
